questions.stem: You want to tell your Japanese class about your exchange trip, event by event in the order things happened. Which text type fits?
options: A report
A postcard
A recount
A notice
questions.explanation: A recount retells past events in sequence, usually with time words and a closing reflection. A report presents findings on a topic, organised by points rather than by time.

questions.stem: Your club needs to tell every student the date, time and place of its first meeting. Which text type fits?
options: A diary entry
A recount
A message
A notice
questions.explanation: A notice is displayed for a general audience and gives the key details of an event or rule. A message is aimed at one person, such as a note of a phone call.

questions.stem: You are on holiday in Hokkaido and want to send your teacher a short greeting with a picture of the snow. Which text type fits?
options: A postcard
An article
A report
A notice
questions.explanation: A postcard is short, sent from a place you are visiting, and tells the reader what you are doing there. An article is written for publication to a wide readership.

questions.stem: You take a phone call for your host mother while she is out. Which message gives her what she needs?
options: 「田中さんはとても元気な人ですね。ぼくもまた会いたいと思いました。」
「あとで田中さんに電話してあげましょうか。」
「三時ごろ田中さんから電話がありました。あとでまた電話するそうです。」
「三時ごろお母さんに電話がありました。とても楽しい話をしました。」
questions.explanation: A phone message must say who called, when and what happens next, here that Tanaka will ring back, reported with 「そうです」. The second option gives a time but not the caller, so the host mother cannot act on it.

questions.stem: In a message passing on what a caller said, which ending shows you are reporting someone else's words?
options: 「明日のよやくは十時かもしれません。」
「明日のよやくは十時になったそうです。」
「明日のよやくは十時にしましょう。」
「明日のよやくは十時がいいと思います。」
questions.explanation: FF + 「そうです」 reports what someone else said, so the reader knows the information came from the caller. 「〜と思います」 turns it into the writer's own opinion.

questions.stem: Which is typical of a note left on the table for a family member?
options: 「はいけい 春になりましたが、お元気ですか。けいぐ」
「みなさん、こんにちは。今日は私の家族についてお話しします。」
「アンケートのけっか、多くの学生が毎日本を読んでいることがわかった。」
「お母さんへ 友だちの家に行ってきます。六時までに帰ります。ケン」
questions.explanation: A note is brief and practical: who it is for, the key information and the writer's name. 「はいけい」 and 「けいぐ」 belong to a formal letter, and the others are a speech opening and a report finding.

questions.stem: Which style suits a note to your younger brother?
options: A seasonal greeting followed by the date
Short, plain forms such as 「先に出かけるよ。」
Formal である style, as in a report
Respectful forms with くださる and いただく
questions.explanation: A note within the family is casual, so plain forms and a friendly sentence-final particle suit it. Respectful language would sound oddly distant to a younger brother.

questions.stem: Which sentence best opens a recount?
options: 「海に行くのはとても楽しいと思います。」
「来週の土曜日、家族と海に行くつもりです。」
「海に行く時は、気をつけてください。」
「先週の土曜日、家族と海に行きました。」
questions.explanation: A recount opens by setting when, who and where, and it is in the past tense. The third option is about a future plan, so it cannot begin a retelling of events.

questions.stem: Which word moves a recount on to the next event?
options: 「それから」
「たとえば」
「でも」
「だから」
questions.explanation: 「それから」 means 'after that', the core sequencing word of a recount. 「たとえば」 gives an example and 「でも」 introduces a contrast.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best close a recount of a school trip?
options: 「朝八時に学校を出て、みんなでバスに乗って、山に行きました。」
「旅行は来月の三日から五日までですから、わすれないでください。」
「旅行に行く人は、お金を持ってきてください。」
「つかれましたが、いろいろなことをならって、ほんとうに楽しい旅行でした。」
questions.explanation: A recount usually ends by reflecting on the experience as a whole. The bus journey is an event from the middle, and the last two sentences belong in a notice.

questions.stem: In a private diary entry, which sentence ending is most usual?
options: Requests, such as 「〜てください」
Plain forms, such as 「今日はいそがしかった。」
Very polite forms, such as 「でございます」
Commands, such as 「はやくしなさい」
questions.explanation: A diary is written for oneself, so plain forms are normal; polite です/ます style is also seen, but very polite forms aimed at a reader are not. Commands and requests need a reader to act on them.

questions.stem: Which word is a common heading for a notice giving information?
options: 「はいけい」
「ただいま」
「おしらせ」
「けいぐ」
questions.explanation: 「おしらせ」 means 'notice' or 'announcement' and often heads a poster or newsletter item. 「はいけい」 and 「けいぐ」 open and close formal letters.

questions.stem: Which sentence is typical of a notice setting out a rule?
options: 「じてんしゃはとてもべんりだと思う。」
「じてんしゃ、ありがとう。またね。」
「ここにじてんしゃをとめないでください。」
「きのう、ここにじてんしゃをとめました。」
questions.explanation: Notices state rules with polite requests such as ない base + 「ないでください」. The second sentence recounts a past event and the third gives an opinion.

questions.stem: Your school notice about a lost umbrella must tell readers what to do. Which sentence does this?
options: 「かさは青くて、とても大きくて、名前はありません。」
「かさがなくて、雨の日はとてもこまっています。」
「先週の金曜日は雨でした。」
「心あたりのある人は、しょくいんしつまで来てください。」
questions.explanation: A notice should end with the action readers are asked to take, here to come to the staffroom if they know anything. Describing the umbrella helps, but it does not tell anyone what to do.

questions.stem: Which sentences fit a postcard from a holiday?
options: 「北海道の人口は多くないことがわかった。」
「北海道へ行く人は、ここで名前を書いてください。」
「北海道について、みなさんにお話しします。」
「今、北海道に来ています。毎日スキーをしています。」
questions.explanation: A postcard is written while away, often with 「〜ています」 to describe where you are and what you are doing now. The others read as a report finding, a notice and a speech opening.

questions.stem: You are writing a postcard to your Japanese teacher. Which opening suits the audience?
options: 「京都、さいこう！またね！」
「先生、お元気ですか。私は今、京都に来ています。」
「先生、元気？今、京都にいるよ。楽しいよ。」
「はいけい 先生におかれましてはますます」
questions.explanation: A teacher is owed polite です/ます style, even in a short postcard. The plain, chatty opening suits a close friend, and the formal letter phrase is far too stiff for a postcard.

questions.stem: In a traditional Japanese letter, where do the date and the writer's name usually go?
options: At the top right, before the greeting
Straight after 「はいけい」 on the first line
Only on the back of the envelope
After the main text, near the end
questions.explanation: Japanese letters put the date, the writer's name and the reader's name after the body and the closing. Starting with the date at the top follows the English pattern.

questions.stem: In an email to your teacher asking about homework, what belongs in the subject line?
options: A seasonal greeting such as 「春になりましたね」 to start
A closing phrase such as 「よろしくおねがいします」
A short summary of the matter, such as 「しゅくだいについてのしつもん」
Your full name, your class and today's date in Japanese
questions.explanation: The subject line tells the reader at a glance what the email is about. Greetings and closing phrases belong in the body, not the subject line.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more suitable for a newspaper article than for a diary?
options: 「シドニーで、日本の文化のイベントがあり、千人ぐらいが来た。」
「今日はほんとうに楽しくて、また行きたいと思った。」
「つかれたから、今日ははやくねよう。」
「あした、友だちに会うのが楽しみだ。」
questions.explanation: An article reports what happened, where and to how many people, in an impersonal voice. The others centre on the writer's own feelings and plans, which is what a diary records.

questions.stem: Which phrase introduces the findings of a survey in a report?
options: 「では、またね。」
「アンケートのけっか、」
「むかしむかし、」
「お元気ですか。」
questions.explanation: 「アンケートのけっか」 means 'the results of the survey', the usual way to present findings, often followed by 「〜ことがわかった」. 「むかしむかし」 opens a folk tale.

questions.stem: What is the usual structure of a report?
options: Events in time order, then personal feelings
Speaker names, questions and answers
Purpose, findings and a conclusion or recommendation
A greeting, then personal news, then a seasonal farewell
questions.explanation: A report states its purpose, sets out findings and ends with a conclusion or recommendation. Events in time order describe a recount, and speaker names with questions and answers describe an interview script.

questions.stem: How is an interview script laid out?
options: As one long paragraph, with no speaker names shown
As a list of the questions only, leaving out answers
With the date and a seasonal greeting at the very top
Each line begins with the speaker's name and a colon
questions.explanation: A script shows who is speaking by putting the name, often shortened, before each line. Without names the reader cannot tell the interviewer from the person interviewed.

questions.stem: Which line would close an interview script?
options: 「はじめまして。どうぞよろしく。」
「では、一つ目のしつもんです。」
「どうしてこの仕事を始めたんですか。」
「今日はどうもありがとうございました。」
questions.explanation: The interviewer ends by thanking the person for their time. The other lines belong at the start or in the middle of the interview.

questions.stem: What makes the script of a speech different from an article on the same topic?
options: It begins with a headline and quotes several written sources
It ends with the date and the writer's name at the bottom
It addresses listeners directly and signposts its points aloud
It is written in plain である style throughout for a wide readership
questions.explanation: A speech speaks to an audience, with 「みなさん」 and spoken signposts such as 「まず」 and 「さいごに」. A headline and quoted sources are features of an article.

questions.stem: How is 「明日は行けない。」 written in polite style?
options: 「明日は行きません。」
「明日は行けません。」
「明日は行かないです。」
「明日は行けなかった。」
questions.explanation: The polite form of the potential negative 「行けない」 is 「行けません」. 「行きません」 drops the potential, so it says 'I won't go' rather than 'I can't go'.

questions.stem: Which writer would most suitably use plain forms with 「よ」 and 「ね」?
options: A student giving a speech at assembly
A student texting a message to a close friend
A student emailing a host family for the first time
A principal writing a notice to parents
questions.explanation: Plain forms and spoken particles suit casual messages between friends. A first email to a host family, a notice to parents and a speech all call for polite style.

questions.stem: On 「げんこうようし」, where does the title go?
options: On the first line, starting in the very first square
Beside the writer's name at the bottom
On the first line, after two or three empty squares
On the last line of the page
questions.explanation: The title goes on the first line, indented by a few squares, and the name comes on the line after. Starting a line in the first square is what you avoid when beginning a paragraph.

questions.stem: On 「げんこうようし」, how is the writer's name set out?
options: On the first line, before the title, starting in the first square
On the last line of the page, centred under the text
On the first line, after the title, in the last squares
On the second line, towards the bottom, with one empty square after it
questions.explanation: The name goes on the line after the title, ending one square from the bottom, with a square between family name and given name. The body of the text starts on the next line.

questions.stem: On 「げんこうようし」, how is a small kana such as 「っ」 or 「ゃ」 written?
options: Written full size, so it is easy for the reader to see
In its own square, in the upper-right part when writing down the page
Squeezed into the square of the kana before it
In the margin beside the line, written half size
questions.explanation: Small kana take a full square of their own, written small; in vertical writing they sit in the upper right of that square. Squeezing them in with the kana before is a common error.
